name: Gola
confidence_why: Westermann 1921 and Koroma 1994 both describe Gola as a tone language with high, mid and low tones plus contour tones on every syllable and both put noun stress on the first stem syllable; they differ only on whether stress in verbs follows the high tone, which Koroma 1994 leaves open pending a full tone analysis.
catalog_citation: Westermann, Diedrich. 1921. Die Gola-Sprache in Liberia: Grammatik, Texte und Wörterbuch. Hamburg: L. Friederichsen. (archive.org item diegolasprachein04west, djvu text layer)
catalog_locator: sec. 31 'Der Starkton', p. 23; tone system sec. 23 'Tonhöhe', p. 19; sentence tone sec. 29, p. 22
catalog_quote: [sec. 23] Jede Silbe und auch manche auslautende Nasale und l haben eine ihnen eigentümliche Tonhöhe. Zu unterscheiden sind die Einzeltöne: Hoch-, Mittel- und Tiefton und vier zusammengesetzte: Hochtief-, Tiefhoch-, Hochmittel- und Mittelhochton. ... [sec. 31 Der Starkton] Wie sich aus Obigem ergibt, tritt der Starkton häufig in enger Verbindung mit der Tonhöhe auf, und zwar fällt er in der Regel mit einem Hochton zusammen. Steht ein Hw ohne Affixe, so kommt ein Starkton nur in Betracht, wenn es mehr als eine Silbe hat: in diesen Fällen hat die erste Silbe ohne Rücksicht auf ihre Tonhöhe einen leichten Starkton. Das Präfix hat ebenfalls Starkton; wird nun infolge des hochtonigen Präfixes die erste Stammsilbe des Hw tieftonig, so behält sie doch ihren Starkton bei. Bei den Formenbildungen des Zw hat die hochtonige Silbe zugleich einen Starkton; dies tritt besonders deutlich bei den Hocht…

new_statements.quote: Westermann geht von einer Bindung an den Hochton aus, beschreibt aber, daß dies nur für Verben, nicht aber für Nomina gelte. Bei zweisilbigen Nomina sei die erste Silbe betont, oder, wenn das Nomen mit Klassenpräfix verwendet wird, die erste Stammsilbe. Bei Verben sei demgegenüber die hochtonige Silbe die betonte. Meinen Beobachtungen zufolge, besteht - unabhängig vom Ton - eine ausgeprägte Tendenz, die erste Stammsilbe sowohl bei zwei- als auch bei dreisilbigen Nomina zu betonen. [...] Eine verbindliche Entscheidung über die Vorhersagbarkeit des Akzents kann wohl nicht ohne eine detaillierte Tonanalyse getroffen werden.
new_statements.translation: [Preceding sentence: 'It is an open question whether the stress accent (Druckakzent) in Gola is bound to tone or not.'] Westermann assumes a binding to high tone, but describes that this holds only for verbs, not for nouns. In disyllabic nouns the first syllable is said to be stressed, or, when the noun is used with a class prefix, the first stem syllable. In verbs, by contrast, the high-toned syllable is said to be the stressed one. According to my observations there is - independently of tone - a marked tendency to stress the first stem syllable in both disyllabic and trisyllabic nouns. [...] A binding decision about the predictability of the accent can probably not be made without a detailed tone analysis.
new_statements.citation: Koroma, Regine. 1994. Die Morphosyntax des Gola. (Afrikanistische Monographien 4.) Köln: Institut für Afrikanistik, Universität zu Köln. xiv+215 pp. ISBN 9783929777031.
new_statements.locator: §2.5 Akzent, p. 21 (PDF page 17, right-hand page of the 2-up scan); tone in §2.6 Ton, pp. 21-23; verb tone §3.2.1.3, p. 42
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (lines 1549-1565) and rendered PDF page 17 of 2-up scan; right-hand page carries printed page number 21, heading '2.5 AKZENT'). The quoted German passage is there word for word; the reader's '[..]' elides only the example list (dɔmã 'road', dɔã 'year', feemã 'Zwischenraum', gbɛwɛ 'backyard' — tone/nasal diacritics are not legible enough in the scan or scanned to fix, as the reader already flagged) and the exceptions sentence about high-falling nouns (kpa'la 'headtie', zo'ɔɔ 'old man', nɔ'goo 'potatoe leaves'), which the reader reports separately under exceptions_mentioned. The preceding sentence ('Es ist eine offene Frage, ob der Druckakzent im Gola an den Ton gebunden ist oder nicht…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has Gola with an empty rule and no existing statements. Koroma 1994 supplies a first explicit statement: tone language with a stress tendency on the first stem syllable of nouns (prefix excluded), verbs reportedly stress the high-toned syllable (Westermann 1921), predictability left open. This fills the empty rule rather than contradicting anything.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gola is a terraced-level tone language (two register tones, downstep; tone is lexically and grammatically distinctive, §2.6). On top of tone, Koroma reports a strong tendency for stress (Druckakzent) to fall on the first stem syllable of nouns (di- and trisyllabic), independent of tone — the class prefix is skipped, so the stressed syllable is the first syllable of the stem. She cites Westermann 1921 for stress on the high-toned syllable in verbs, and leaves open whether stress is bound to tone. Examples given (scanned-garbled tone marks): dɔmá 'road', dɔá 'year', feemá 'gap/space', gbɛwɛ 'backyard'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Es gibt jedoch einige Ausnahmen, u.a. einige Nomina mit Hoch-Falltonmuster wie kpa'la 'headtie', zɔ'ɔɔ 'old man' oder nɔɔ'gɔɔ 'potatoe leaves'' — some nouns with a high-falling tone pattern do not take initial stem stress (p. 21). Verbs, per Westermann, stress the high-toned syllable rather than the first. Koroma stresses that the predictability of accent cannot be settled without a full tone analysis, which the book does not provide (it writes data without tones, p. 22).
new_statements.identity_note: Koroma describes the Gola of Sierra Leone (eight months of fieldwork in 1991; the dedication names a consultant from Tahn); she names dialects Kongba, Goje, Tee and Deng in the phonology chapter but the accent statement is not dialect-specific. Westermann 1921, whom she relays for verb stress, describes the Gola of Liberia.

readall_conflicts: Only one work was listed and opened, so there is no disagreement between opened sources. Within Koroma 1994 there is an internal tension she reports rather than resolves: Westermann (1921) ties stress to high tone in verbs (stressed syllable = high-toned syllable) but not in nouns, whereas Koroma's own observation is that noun stress falls on the first stem syllable regardless of tone, with exceptions among nouns bearing a high-falling pattern; she explicitly says the question of whether stress is bound to tone is open and cannot be decided without a detailed tone analysis (which she does not provide; Sindlinger 1975b, an unpublished Monrovia manuscript, is cited as the phonology/tonology source).

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in the held source, confirmed against the archive.org page images (printed pp. 19 and 23, secs. 23 and 31) and the djvu text layer; locators correct. (2) Deciding source: Westermann 1921, a primary grammar sketch with texts and dictionary (vii+178 pp) that has explicit sections on lexical/grammatical tone and on 'Starkton'; the classification 'tonal' (H/M/L plus contours; stress secondary, coinciding with H; light initial stress on polysyllabic affixless nouns noted as the primary-stress rule) follows directly from it. (3) Better sources: Glottolog lists Koroma 1994 (morphosyntax, print only) and Sindlinger's unpublished 1975 phonology/grammar manuscripts (archival); no instrumental/JIPA/recent phonology work was found (Crossref empty; 2025 Oxford Guide to Atlantic languages has no Gola chapter; WALS cites only Koroma for non-prosodic features).
